column4: The source section’s root خ ش ع names the lowered face and a worshipper’s bow; here خَاشِعَةً أَبْصَارُهُمْ is joined to the call to prostrate while they had been سالمون, making voluntary worship and judgment-day humiliation meet.
The source section links the root ص ل ي in entering fire with ritual prayer; this answer says لَمْ نَكُ مِنَ الْمُصَلِّينَ, and 74:42 supplies the question that places the answer in Saqar.
The source section says خاشع also names the one who bows in prayer; this describes believers as خَاشِعُونَ in their prayer, a voluntary devotional posture set against the humbled faces of 88:2.
The source section explicitly pairs its root ص ل ي senses: this ayah says يَصْلَى النار الكبرى, the fire-entry sense, beside 87:15’s prayer sense.
The source section explicitly pairs this root’s senses: here one remembers his Lord and then فَصَلَّىٰ, the prayer sense, set against the fire-entry in 87:12.
The source section directly cites فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّىٰ; the negated prayer is the same ص ل ي word-family whose other branch in 88:4 means entering fire.
The source section directly cites كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ and connects turning away to 88:23; this ayah’s denial and turning away specify the stance paired with failure to pray in 75:31.
The source section’s fire-entry root ص ل ي recurs in لَا يَصْلَاهَا; this passage makes burning a boundary, with 92:16 identifying the denier who turns away.
The source section links 88:23’s turning away and disbelief with 75:32; this ayah repeats كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ, while 92:15 supplies its own passage’s fire consequence.
The source section’s root ن ص ب is glossed as standing until weariness and this verse is cited directly: فَانصَبْ commands the addressed Prophet to exert himself once free.
The source section’s root خ ش ع describes the bowed face; these wrongdoers are خَاشِعِينَ مِنَ الذُّلِّ as they are exposed to the Fire, an explicit judgment-day humiliation.

This verse joins prayer with الخَاشِعِينَ and says it is burdensome except for them; it sharpens the source section’s pairing of prayer-posture and weary labor by giving humility a different relation to prayer.
The source section glosses خاشع as including a raki, one who bows; this command explicitly joins prayer to وَارْكَعُوا مَعَ الرَّاكِعِينَ, bowing with the worshippers.
The source section reads نَاصِبَة through upright, tiring posture; here the maintained prayers are paired with وَقُومُوا لِلَّهِ قَانِتِينَ, standing devoutly before God.
The source section names prayer as comprising bowing and prostration; this verse names both postures, الرُّكَّعِ السُّجُودِ, in the purified House.
The source section connects a bowed face with the raki and prayer’s bodily acts; Mary is told to prostrate and bow, وَاسْجُدِي وَارْكَعِي, as worship.
The source section’s weary upright posture and prayer’s prostration meet in this community that stands reciting by night and is وَهُمْ يَسْجُدُونَ, a willing devotional scene.
When the Merciful’s signs are recited, these servants fall سُجَّدًا وَبُكِيًّا; their chosen prostration and tears contrast with the forced call and humiliation in 68:43.
The source section links an upright, tiring body to ritual prayer; these servants spend the night سُجَّدًا وَقِيَامًا before their Lord, joining prostration and standing as willing worship.
This command to bow and prostrate, ارْكَعُوا وَاسْجُدُوا, gives the bodily prayer postures that the source section hears behind its words for bowed faces and burning.

The source section contrasts a worldly invitation to prostrate with the later humiliating call; here people refuse the worldly command اسْجُدُوا لِلرَّحْمَٰنِ, clarifying the voluntary side of that boundary.
The source section joins face and prayer posture; this verse makes prostration visible on believers’ faces, سِيمَاهُمْ فِي وُجُوهِهِم مِّنْ أَثَرِ السُّجُودِ, as a mark of worship.
The imperative وَاسْجُدْ وَاقْتَرِبْ makes prostration a willing approach to God, the devotional counterpart to the compelled prostration described in 68:43.

This asks whether one who spends the night prostrating and standing, سَاجِدًا وَقَائِمًا, fearing the Hereafter, is like one who does not; it links the source section’s prayer-postures to the judgment that separates faces.
The source section says the root ذ ك ر includes prayer; this command joins إقامة الصلاة to لِذِكْرِي, prayer explicitly performed for God’s remembrance.
The source section brings bowed humility and remembrance together; this ayah asks believers’ hearts to تَخْشَعَ لِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ, directly joining the root خ ش ع to dhikr.
The source section’s root خ ش ع includes devotional bowing; here listeners fall on their faces weeping and خُشُوعًا increases, a chosen response unlike the later humiliation.
The section’s account of dhikr includes supplication, and it names خاشع; here servants call on God and are described as خَاشِعِينَ, voluntary humility before the day’s humiliation.
This verse places الخَاشِعِينَ and those who remember God often, الذَّاكِرِينَ اللَّهَ كَثِيرًا, among the same believing qualities, meeting two roots the source section names.
This verse brings remembrance and prayer into one account of believers: God’s mention moves their hearts, and they يُقِيمُونَ الصَّلَاةَ; it clarifies the source section’s prayer/remembrance link.
The source section says dhikr may mean prayer; this verse commands prayer and then says وَلَذِكْرُ اللَّهِ أَكْبَرُ, placing the two acts in an explicit relation.
When Friday prayer is called, people are told فَاسْعَوْا إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ; this joins prayer and remembrance, as in the source section’s secondary sense of dhikr.
This ayah itself stages the judgment-day call to prostrate and inability to do so; 68:43, the source section’s cited neighbor, adds the lowered eyes and the memory of being sound.
The question أَيُّ شَيْءٍ سَلَكَكُمْ فِي سَقَرَ names the fire that 74:43 answers by naming the absence of prayer; its contribution is to frame prayer as an answer about entry into Saqar.
Those punished are يَسْحَبُونَ فِي النَّارِ عَلَىٰ وُجُوهِهِمْ; the face carried into fire joins the source section’s bowed faces and burning as a stark forced posture.
Here the fire burns their faces, تَلْفَحُ وُجُوهَهُمُ النَّارُ, joining the source section’s separate face and fire images in one punishment scene.
People are gathered عَلَىٰ وُجُوهِهِمْ إِلَىٰ جَهَنَّمَ; the face directed toward punishment links the bowed face with the fire-bound body in the source section.
This asks about one who shields his face from the worst punishment on Judgment Day; it makes the face itself the site of exposure to the consequence paired with 88:2, 88:3, and 88:4.
On the day they emerge from graves, their eyes are خَاشِعَةٌ and humiliation covers them; the same rooted lowering on judgment day extends the source section’s bowed face.
The scene gives humiliated eyes, أَبْصَارُهَا خَاشِعَةٌ, using the source section’s root for a face lowered at the Resurrection.
The dead come from graves with خُشَّعًا أَبْصَارُهُمْ; the same root and lowered gaze place the section’s bowed-face image in another Resurrection scene.
At the Resurrection the voices خَشَعَتْ لِلرَّحْمَٰنِ; the source section applies khushu to faces and prayer, while this ayah transfers that abasement to sound.
The resurrected rush as if toward a نُصُبٍ, an erected object; the source section’s root ن ص ب names upright standing until fatigue, while 70:44 adds the lowered eyes and humiliation.
After prayer, believers remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides; this ayah itself continues prayer into dhikr through bodily states, the relation the source section’s lexical note raises.

The Prophet and believers are described standing long portions of the night, then given relief and told to recite what is easy and establish prayer; this makes the source section’s tiring upright stance concrete.
This generation أَضَاعُوا الصَّلَاةَ and followed desires; the loss of prayer gives a specific negative counterpart to the source section’s link between prayer and the burned.
After 92:15 and 92:16 describe who burns and why, this ayah’s own contribution is that the most God-conscious will be kept away from that same fire, a boundary in the section’s burning image.

The source section’s root خ ش ع describes a bowed face and worshipper; here a mountain would be خَاشِعًا before God’s revelation and split from fear, showing the same root applied beyond the human prayer-body.
